summary: A long, narrow country stretching more than 4,000 kilometers along the western coast of South America, with the Atacama Desert in the north and Patagonia in the south, known for its copper mines, wine and stable economic development.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism arrived with the founding of Santiago in 1541 by the Spanish conquistador Pedro de Valdivia and was the only legal religion in the colonial period. After Chile's independence in 1818 Catholicism remained the state religion, until the 1925 constitution formally separated church and state. During the Pinochet military regime of 1973–1990, the Catholic Church set up the Vicariate of Solidarity to protect victims of human-rights abuses and enjoyed high social prestige; but the clergy sexual-abuse scandals that erupted in 2018 severely damaged the church, and its share has continued to fall.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has grown rapidly in recent decades, especially among the younger generation and in large cities. After democratization in 1990 society gradually liberalized, and on issues such as the legalization of divorce in 2004 and the partial decriminalization of abortion in 2017, society and the church took divergent positions; together with the church sexual-abuse scandals of 2018, this led many people to leave the church, and the share of non-religious people has risen to about 30%.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Evangelical)
ranking.description: Protestantism arrived in the 19th century with German and British immigrants and American missionaries; in 1909 the Methodist pastor Willis Hoover started a Pentecostal revival in Valparaíso and founded the Methodist Pentecostal Church of Chile, one of the earliest Pentecostal movements in Latin America. In the 20th century Pentecostalism grew rapidly among the urban poor and working class, and since 2008 Chile has designated October 31 a national holiday, the 'Day of the Evangelical and Protestant Churches'.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: Other religions include Judaism, Islam, Jehovah's Witnesses and Mormonism, as well as the traditional beliefs of the indigenous Mapuche. The Mapuche worship ancestral spirits and nature spirits, and religious ceremonies are led by female shamans, the 'machi', for example the New Year festival 'We Tripantu' (around June 24).

religion.background: Before the arrival of the Spanish, Chile's indigenous peoples such as the Mapuche and the Aymara had their own ancestral-spirit and nature beliefs. After Spanish colonization in 1541, Catholicism arrived with the conquistadors and missionaries, but the Mapuche in the south long resisted Spanish rule and were only incorporated when the Chilean government launched the war known as the 'Pacification of Araucanía' in the late 19th century. The 1925 constitution separated church and state, and in the 20th century Pentecostalism expanded among the working class. During the military regime of 1973–1990 the church became a force protecting human rights, and after democratization in 1990 secularization accelerated.

language.official: The official language is, de facto, Spanish.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish arrived with Spanish colonization in 1541; in the colonial period it was the language of administration and the Church, and after independence in 1818 it became the national language. Chilean Spanish is known for its fast speech and heavy use of slang (such as 'cachai' and 'po'). Because indigenous languages shrank greatly under colonization, the wars of the 19th century and assimilation policies, Spanish has become the mother tongue of about 99% of the population.

ranking.name: Mapuche (Mapudungun)
ranking.description: Mapuche (Mapudungun) is the language of the Mapuche of the south, who successfully resisted the Spanish for three hundred years in the colonial period; in 1641 Spain and the Mapuche signed the Treaty of Quillín, recognizing autonomy south of the Biobío River. But after the Chilean government militarily occupied Araucanía in the late 19th century, the Mapuche lost their land and were forcibly assimilated, the number of Mapuche speakers fell sharply, and today only about 1% of the population can use it fluently.

language.history: Before the arrival of the Spanish, Chile had many indigenous languages: Aymara and Quechua in the north, Mapuche in the center and south, and languages such as Yaghan at the southern tip. From 1541 the Spanish colonized, and Spanish became the dominant language. In the 19th century the Chilean government promoted national education centered on Spanish, and after conquering Araucanía in the late 19th century it accelerated the assimilation of the Mapuche. The 1993 Indigenous Law began to recognize indigenous languages and cultures and promoted bilingual education programs, but many indigenous languages are on the verge of disappearing; for example, the last native speaker of Yaghan died in 2022.

ranking.name: Empanada de pino
ranking.description: A baked half-moon pastry filled with 'pino', ground beef stir-fried with plenty of onion, with a black olive, a boiled egg and raisins added.
ranking.history: The empanada de pino derives from the Spanish empanada and arrived with Spanish colonization in the 16th century; the word 'pino' may derive from the Mapuche 'pinu' (fragment). It is most popular during the national holiday of September 18 (Fiestas Patrias, commemorating the establishment of the first Government Junta in 1810), when every household buys or makes them. At Sunday family lunches, empanadas are also a common starter.

ranking.name: Pastel de choclo (corn pie)
ranking.description: Sweet corn is ground into a purée and mixed with basil, spread over ground beef, chicken, olives and boiled egg, and baked in a clay bowl until the surface is golden.
ranking.history: Pastel de choclo combines the indigenous corn diet with the meat, olives and eggs brought by the Spanish, a representative dish of colonial-era fusion cooking. The word 'choclo' comes from Quechua and means fresh corn. It is the most popular home-cooked dish in Chile's summer corn harvest season (January–March), traditionally baked and served in a clay bowl (paila de greda), and the bowls from the central Chilean pottery town of Pomaire are the most famous.

ranking.name: Cazuela
ranking.description: A clear stew of beef, chicken or pork cooked with potato, pumpkin, corn and rice or thin noodles, in which each person's bowl holds a large piece of meat and whole vegetables.
ranking.history: Cazuela derives from the Spanish stew tradition, and its name comes from the Spanish 'cazuela' (earthenware pot), combined with indigenous crops such as corn, potatoes and pumpkin. Because its ingredients are plentiful and filling, it is the most common dish in Chilean households in winter. In rural areas it is also a traditional dish for entertaining guests and for festivals.

ranking.name: Curanto
ranking.description: A pit is dug in the ground and filled with heated stones, then layered with shellfish, meat, sausage, potatoes and bread dough, covered with large leaves and earth, and left to cook.
ranking.history: Curanto is a traditional dish of Chiloé Island in the south, and its name comes from the Mapuche 'kurantu' (stone). The indigenous peoples of Chiloé (the Chono and the Huilliche) long ago cooked seafood in pits with heated stones, and after the arrival of Spanish missionaries and settlers in the 17th–18th centuries, pork, sausage and potato bread were added. Today curanto is an important event in the community festivals of Chiloé and is often prepared collectively by community members.

ranking.name: Completo (Chilean hot dog)
ranking.description: A long soft hot-dog bun filled with a sausage, then topped with plenty of diced tomato, mashed avocado and mayonnaise, sometimes with sauerkraut, a generous portion with a rich taste.
ranking.history: The classic version of the Chilean hot dog, the 'italiano', is named for the red, green and white of tomato, avocado and mayonnaise, which match the colors of the Italian flag. It is said to have been introduced in the 1920s by Eduardo Brown, a Chilean who had worked in the United States, at the restaurant 'Quick Lunch Bahamondes' in Santiago. Chile is one of the world's largest consumers of avocado, and mashed avocado is an indispensable topping of the Chilean hot dog; today it is Chile's most popular fast food.
